title: Mensuration (3D)
summary: Volumes and surface areas of cubes, cuboids, cylinders, cones, spheres, hemispheres, prisms and pyramids, plus melting-recasting, capacities and painted-cube counts. About 1-3 questions per shift; every question reduces to one formula plus a unit conversion, so memorising the formula sheet is nearly the whole job.

subtopics.title: Cube and cuboid
subtopics.concept: A cuboid has three dimensions l, b, h; a cube makes them equal. Volume is the product of the three; surface area adds the six faces. Capacity questions are volume questions with a litres conversion at the end.

formulas.name: Cuboid
formulas.note: l, b, h are the three dimensions.

formulas.name: Painted cube counts
formulas.note: 3, 2, 1, 0 painted faces for n by n by n.

tricks.title: Cubes table, not cube roots
tricks.body: Know the cubes to 12 by heart. Reverse questions become look-ups: 343 is 7 cubed.

mistakes.right: It is $2(lb+bh+hl)$. For $12\times10\times8$ that is 592, not 720.

mistakes.right: One cubic metre is $1000$ litres: $1.2$ m$^3$ is 1200 L.

mistakes.wrong: Doubling the edge and doubling the volume.
mistakes.right: Volume takes the cube of the scale: $2^3=8$ times, so $125\to1000$.

mistakes.wrong: Painted-cube corner counts other than 8.

subtopics.notes:
### The master table
| Quantity | Cuboid $l\times b\times h$ | Cube, edge $a$ |
|---|---|---|
| Volume | $lbh$ | $a^3$ |
| Lateral surface (4 walls) | $2h(l+b)$ | $4a^2$ |
| Total surface (6 faces) | $2(lb+bh+hl)$ | $6a^2$ |
| Diagonal | $\sqrt{l^2+b^2+h^2}$ | $a\sqrt3$ |

Cuboid $12\times10\times8$: volume $960$, walls $2\times8\times22=352$, total surface $2\times(120+80+96)=592$.

Reverse works too: volume $960$ with two dimensions $12$ and $10$ leaves the third as $\dfrac{960}{120}=8$. Attach square units to areas and cubic units to volumes, always.

> **Rule:** Total surface is the walls plus top and bottom. Lateral surface alone skips the two $l\times b$ faces.

### Cube shortcuts
Edge $6$: volume $216$, lateral $144$, total $216$, diagonal $6\sqrt3$. The diagonal formula comes from using the cuboid diagonal with all three sides equal. A cube of volume $216$ has edge $6$; volume $125$ gives edge $5$.

Doubling every edge multiplies area by $4$ and volume by $8$. Edge $5\to10$: total surface $150\to600$, volume $125\to1000$.

> **Tip:** Lengths take $k$, areas $k^2$, volumes $k^3$. Count what kind of quantity is asked before multiplying anything.

### Capacity and cost
One cubic metre holds $1000$ litres, one litre is $1000$ cubic centimetres. A tank $1.5\times1\times0.8$ m has volume $1.2$ m$^3$, which is $1200$ litres.

Cost questions multiply volume by a rate: digging at Rs $20$ per m$^3$ costs $20\times1.2=$ Rs $24$ for that tank. Match the rate's units to the volume's units before multiplying.

> **Watch:** Convert units exactly once, at the end. Mixing cm and m midway is where capacity questions die.

### Reverse questions
Given the volume or surface, peel back to the edge, then forward to the asked quantity.

Volume $343$ cu cm means edge $7$ (since $7^3=343$); total surface is then $6\times49=294$ sq cm. Two steps, no algebra.

> **Remember:** Learn the cubes up to $12$: $1,8,27,64,125,216,343,512,729,1000,1331,1728$. Reverse questions then need no cube roots.

### Painted cubes
An $n\times n\times n$ cube painted outside, cut into unit cubes:
- $3$ faces painted: the $8$ corners
- $2$ faces: the edges, $12(n-2)$
- $1$ face: face centres, $6(n-2)^2$
- $0$ faces: inside, $(n-2)^3$

A $4$ cm cube cut into $1$ cm cubes: $8$, $24$, $24$, $8$. The four counts always add to $n^3=64$. A $3$ cm cube gives $8$, $12$, $6$, $1$.

> **Tip:** Only corner cubes get three faces, always exactly $8$. Start there, then fill the edge and face counts. Slice counts never change when the whole cube is dipped instead of brushed.

subtopics.title: Cylinder
subtopics.concept: A cylinder of radius r and height h has volume pi r squared h and curved surface two pi r h. The total surface adds the two circular ends. Most questions either substitute directly or reverse one dimension from the volume.

formulas.name: Dimension change
formulas.note: Scale each symbol by its own factor.

mistakes.wrong: Using the diameter in $\pi r^2h$.
mistakes.right: Radius only. Diameter $14$ means $r=7$.

mistakes.wrong: Calling the CSA the total surface.
Multiplying cubic metres by 100 for litres.
Scaling volume by $2$ when only the radius doubles.
mistakes.right: $r$ is squared: volume $\times4$. Height halving then brings it to $\times2$.

mistakes.wrong: Re-deriving $\pi r^2$ every line.
mistakes.right: Factor it once ($154$ for $r=7$) and reuse; errors drop sharply.

subtopics.notes:
### The three formulas
$$V=\pi r^2h,\qquad \text{CSA}=2\pi rh,\qquad \text{TSA}=2\pi r(h+r)$$
TSA is the curved surface plus both circles: $2\pi rh+2\pi r^2$.

Radius $7$, height $10$: volume $\dfrac{22}{7}\times49\times10=1540$; CSA $2\times\dfrac{22}{7}\times7\times10=440$; TSA $440+308=748$. Check TSA the second way: $2\pi r(h+r)=2\times\dfrac{22}{7}\times7\times17=748$.

> **Rule:** Fix the radius first and keep it factored. The $r$ cancels out of most reverse questions.

### Reverse: find the missing dimension
Volume $1540$ with radius $7$: $h=\dfrac{1540}{154}=10$, because $\pi r^2=\dfrac{22}{7}\times49=154$. One division, and the same trick answers every reverse question.

The same move finds the radius when the height is given: $r^2=\dfrac{V}{\pi h}$, then recall the square. And the CSA reverses the same way: $440=2\times\dfrac{22}{7}\times7\times h$ gives $h=10$.

> **Tip:** $\pi r^2$ for $r=7$ is $154$; for $r=14$ it is $616$; for $r=21$ it is $1386$. Halves appear too: $r=3.5$ gives $38.5$. These four end up everywhere.

### Pipes, wells and capacity
A hollow pipe or a well uses the same cylinder; a pipe's length plays the height's role. Well of radius $1.4$ m and depth $5$ m:
$$V=\frac{22}{7}\times1.96\times5=30.8\text{ m}^3=30{,}800\text{ litres}$$

Cost of digging multiplies the volume by the rate per cubic metre, exactly like tank questions. At Rs $25$ per m$^3$, that well costs $25\times30.8=$ Rs $770$.

A one-litre bottle holds $1000$ cu cm; the tank and bottle rules are one rule.

> **Watch:** Radius $1.4$ m is $140$ cm if the question mixes units. Pick one unit before the first line.

### Changing the dimensions
- Radius doubled, height same: volume $4$ times, curved surface $2$ times.
- Radius doubled, height halved: volume $2$ times.
- Height alone doubled: volume $2$ times, curved surface $2$ times.
- Radius and height both doubled: volume $8$ times.

The exponent tracks the factor: $r$ appears squared in the volume, once in the curved surface.

> **Remember:** Ask which symbols the change touches. Volume $V=\pi r^2h$: scale $r^2$ by $4$ and $h$ by $\dfrac12$, net $2$.

### Melting into a cylinder
Volume survives a melt. The shape changes; the amount of metal does not. A cone of radius $7$, height $12$ has volume $\dfrac13\times154\times12=616$; poured into a cylinder of radius $7$ it reaches height $\dfrac{616}{154}=4$ cm.

> **Tip:** Melted questions never need the second solid's shape knowledge beyond its volume formula. Equate volumes, solve for one length.

subtopics.title: Cone
subtopics.concept: A cone of radius r and height h has slant height root of r squared plus h squared. Its volume is one third of a cylinder on the same base; its curved surface is pi r l. Radius-height-slant triples are Pythagorean triplets, most often 3-4-5 and 7-24-25.

example.q: A conical tent has base radius 7 m and slant height 25 m. The canvas required to make it (sq m) is:

mistakes.wrong: Using $\pi rh$ for the curved surface.
mistakes.right: It is $\pi r\ell$ with the slant. For 7 and 24 that means 550, not $\pi\times7\times24$.

mistakes.wrong: Treating the slant as the height.
mistakes.right: Height is the drop down the middle; slant runs along the surface. $\ell=\sqrt{r^2+h^2}$.

mistakes.wrong: Forgetting the $\dfrac13$ in the cone volume.
mistakes.right: A cone is one-third of its cylinder: $120$ cylinder means $40$ cone.

mistakes.wrong: Adding the base to a tent's canvas.
mistakes.right: Tents need the curved surface $\pi r\ell$ only.

mistakes.wrong: Cancelling $\pi$ but not the $\dfrac13$ when melting.
mistakes.right: Carry the one-third: $288\pi$ as a sphere gives $R^3=216$, $R=6$.

subtopics.notes:
### The three lengths first
$$\ell=\sqrt{r^2+h^2}$$
Radius $7$ and height $24$ give slant $25$: the $7$-$24$-$25$ triplet. Check for a triplet before squaring anything. Radius $21$ with height $28$ gives slant $35$, and $\dfrac{22}{7}\times21\times35=2310$ sq cm of curved surface.

The three lengths make a right triangle inside the cone: radius and height at right angles, slant along the surface. Families to know: $3$-$4$-$5$ and its multiples, $7$-$24$-$25$, $8$-$15$-$17$, $12$-$35$-$37$.

A classic ratio: cylinder, hemisphere and cone on the same base with cylinder height $=$ radius hold volumes $3:2:1$.

> **Rule:** Find $\ell$ first. Both surface formulas need it, and triplet spotting avoids the root.

### Volume and the one-third
$$V=\frac{1}{3}\pi r^2h$$
Exactly one-third of the cylinder with the same base and height. A cylinder of volume $120$ pairs with a cone of $40$. Radius $7$ with height $9$ gives $V=\dfrac13\times154\times9=462$ cu cm.

The factor $\dfrac13$ also runs in reverse: cone volume $132$ with radius $3$ gives height $\dfrac{132\times3}{\dfrac{22}{7}\times9}=14$ cm.

> **Tip:** Multiply by $3$ before dividing by $\pi r^2$. Keeping the fraction until the end invites slips.

### Surfaces
- Curved surface: $\pi r\ell$. Radius $7$, slant $25$: $\dfrac{22}{7}\times7\times25=550$ sq cm.
- Total surface: $\pi r\ell+\pi r^2$, the skirt plus the circular base. Same cone: $550+154=704$ sq cm.

A conical tent uses the curved surface only: no floor. Canvas for radius $7$ m and slant $25$ m is $550$ sq m. A heap whose base circumference is $44$ m has radius $\dfrac{44\times7}{44}=7$ m, so slant $25$ m again means $550$ sq m of sheet.

> **Watch:** Tents and caps are curved surface; ice-cream cones and solid cones are total surface. Read what is covered.

### Melting a cone
Volume survives. A cone of radius $6$, height $24$ has volume $288\pi$; as a sphere:
$$\frac{4}{3}\pi R^3=288\pi \Rightarrow R^3=216 \Rightarrow R=6$$
The sphere comes out with the same $6$ cm radius, a clean coincidence worth noticing. And $216=6^3$ came straight from the cubes table, not a calculator.

The reverse melt works the same way: a sphere of radius $6$ recast as a cone of radius $6$ needs $\dfrac13\times36\times h=288$, so $h=24$ cm.

### Heaps and tents
A heap of rice is a cone: base circumference gives the radius, slant gives the canvas or sheet. Cloth width questions divide the curved area by the width.

> **Remember:** Cone problems are two-part: the inner right triangle for lengths, then one formula for the asked quantity.

subtopics.title: Sphere and hemisphere
subtopics.concept: A sphere of radius r has volume four-thirds pi r cubed and surface four pi r squared. A hemisphere is half a sphere for volume, but its total surface is three pi r squared because it adds the flat circle. Radius scaling cubes for volume and squares for surface.

subtopics.notes:
### The sphere pair
$$V=\frac{4}{3}\pi r^3,\qquad S=4\pi r^2$$
Radius $7$: surface $4\times154=616$ sq cm; volume $\dfrac43\times\dfrac{22}{7}\times343=\dfrac{4312}{3}\approx1437.3$ cu cm.

Radius $14$: surface $4\times616=2464$ sq cm; volume $\dfrac43\times\dfrac{22}{7}\times2744=\dfrac{34496}{3}$ cu cm, exactly $8$ times the radius-$7$ volume. Radius $3.5$: surface $154$ sq cm, volume $\dfrac{539}{3}\approx179.7$ cu cm.

The surface formula is exactly four circles of the same radius. Half of it, $2\pi r^2$, is the hemisphere's curved part. A sphere also fills exactly two-thirds of the cylinder that tightly contains it.

> **Rule:** Surface grows with $r^2$, volume with $r^3$. Doubling the radius gives $4$ times the surface and $8$ times the volume, as the $7\to14$ line above shows.

### Hemisphere: three halves and three pi
- Volume: $\dfrac{2}{3}\pi r^3$ (half the sphere).
- Curved surface: $2\pi r^2$ (half the shell).
- **Total surface: $3\pi r^2$** because the flat circular face $\pi r^2$ joins the shell.

Radius $7$: curved $308$, total $3\times154=462$, volume $\dfrac{2156}{3}$ cu cm. Radius $21$: curved $2772$, total $4158$, all from the $1386$ base circle.

> **Watch:** 'Total surface of a hemisphere' is $3\pi r^2$, never $2\pi r^2$. The flat face counts once it is solid.

### Melting and dividing
A sphere of radius $6$ melted into $8$ equal small spheres: each carries $\dfrac{216}{8}=27$ of the cubed length, so each radius is $3$.

Count multiplies the volume, so the radius shrinks by the cube root of the count. Eight pieces mean half the radius; $27$ pieces mean one-third; counts $1,8,27$ pair with radius factors $1,\dfrac12,\dfrac13$.

> **Tip**: When a big solid becomes $n$ equal small ones, divide the cubed length by $n$, then take the cube root.

### Displacing water
A solid dropped in a full tub pushes out its own volume. Sphere of radius $3$ in a full tank: overflow $=\dfrac43\pi\times27=36\pi$ cu cm.

In a partly filled cylinder the level rises instead: sphere of radius $7$ into a cylinder of radius $14$ raises the water by $\dfrac{4312/3}{616}=\dfrac73$ cm. Read the story: 'water level rose' means the rise's cylinder volume equals the sphere's volume.

### Radius ratios
Radii $3:4$ give volumes $27:64$ and surfaces $9:16$. Cube the ratio for volumes, square it for surfaces, and say which one the question wants. Equal surfaces force equal radii; equal volumes likewise.

> **Remember:** Ratio questions never need pi. Cancel it first, then compare powers of the ratio.

subtopics.concept: A prism's volume is base area times height; a pyramid's is one third of that. Frustums interpolate between two circular ends. Cutting and melting questions conserve volume, and painted or cut cubes follow counting formulas.

formulas.name: Frustum
formulas.note: R, r = the two end radii.

formulas.name: Lateral surfaces
formulas.note: P = base perimeter; L = length; slant for pyramid.

tricks.title: One-third rule of thumb
tricks.body: Same base and height: pyramid = one third of the prism. Use it to sanity-check any answer.

mistakes.wrong: Using the full prism volume for a pyramid.
mistakes.right: The pyramid takes one-third: $\dfrac13\times100\times12=400$, not 1200.

mistakes.wrong: Dropping the $Rr$ term in a frustum.
mistakes.right: Radii $5$ and $3$ need $25+9+15=49$; without $Rr$ it is only 34.

mistakes.wrong: Using the slant edge as the pyramid height.
mistakes.right: Volume needs the perpendicular height; slant heights serve the lateral surface.

mistakes.wrong: Adding the cube edges when melting.
Prism lateral with the slant height.
mistakes.right: Prisms have no slant; lateral $=$ perimeter $\times$ length.

subtopics.notes:
### Prism: base times length
$$V=\text{base area}\times\text{length}$$
A triangular prism with cross-section $20$ sq cm and length $12$ cm holds $240$ cu cm. A rectangular base $7\times5$ with length $10$ holds $350$ cu cm.

The base can be a triangle, square, hexagon, anything regular. Find its area first, multiply by the length second. A cuboid is just a prism with a rectangle base, so the tank formula lives here too.

> **Rule:** The prism formula needs exactly two things: the base area and the prism length. Everything else is decoration.

### Pyramid: a third of the prism
$$V=\frac{1}{3}\times\text{base area}\times\text{height}$$
Square base $10$, height $12$: $V=\dfrac13\times100\times12=400$ cu cm. Rectangular base $9\times4$ with height $7$: $V=\dfrac13\times36\times7=84$ cu cm.

Same base, same height: the pyramid always holds one-third of the prism's volume. The cone's one-third is the same idea on a circular base.

When a face slant of $13$ sits on a base of side $10$, the half-base is $5$, so the true height is $\sqrt{169-25}=12$. Slant first, height second.

> **Tip:** The pyramid height is the perpendicular drop to the base centre, never the slant edge.

### Frustum: the bucket shape
A cone with its top sliced off. With radii $R$ (bottom) and $r$ (top), height $h$:
$$V=\frac{\pi h}{3}\left(R^2+r^2+Rr\right)$$
Radii $5$ and $3$, height $6$: $\dfrac{22}{7}\times\dfrac{6}{3}\times(25+9+15)=\dfrac{44}{7}\times49=308$ cu cm.

A frustum is a big cone minus the small cone sliced off, and similar triangles link the two radii. Slant height $\sqrt{h^2+(R-r)^2}$: with radii $8$ and $3$ and height $12$ it is $\sqrt{144+25}=13$, the $5$-$12$-$13$ triplet again.

> **Watch:** The cross term $Rr$ is the one students drop. Three terms, always: $R^2$, $r^2$, $Rr$.

### Melting cubes
Three cubes of edges $3$, $4$, $5$ melt into one cube. Volume adds: $27+64+125=216=6^3$, so the new edge is $6$ cm.

Melting adds volumes, then one cube root. The cube table turns this into arithmetic. Splitting runs the other way: one cube of edge $12$ gives $8$ cubes of edge $6$, since $\dfrac{1728}{8}=216=6^3$.

### Lateral surfaces
- Prism: perimeter of base $\times$ length.
- Pyramid: $\dfrac12\times$ perimeter of base $\times$ slant height.

Square pyramid, base $10$, slant $13$: $\dfrac12\times40\times13=260$ sq cm. The slant height belongs to each triangular face.

Triangular prism with base sides $6$, $8$, $10$ and length $12$: perimeter $24$, so lateral $=24\times12=288$ sq cm. The base is a right triangle by the $6$-$8$-$10$ test.

> **Remember:** Prism lateral uses the length; pyramid lateral uses the slant height. Check which one the question gives.

patterns.howToSpot: Several solids melted into one, or one cube cut into many.
steps: Add all volumes (or divide for pieces).
Equate to the target solid's volume formula.

patterns.howToSpot: A side surface asked, with perimeter and slant data.

example.q: A square pyramid has a base of side 10 cm and slant height 13 cm. Its lateral surface area is:

revision: Prism: base area $\times$ length.
Pyramid: one-third of the same-base prism volume.
Frustum: $\dfrac{\pi h}{3}(R^2+r^2+Rr)$; keep all three terms.
Melting: add volumes, then take the cube root for an edge.
Lateral: prism $P\times L$; pyramid $\dfrac12 P\ell$ with the slant.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Length, breadth and height of a box are given. Volume or surface area is asked.
pyqPatterns.approach:
Volume = length × breadth × height.
Surface = 2 × (sum of the three different face areas).

example.q: Find the total surface area of a cuboid 12 × 10 × 8 cm.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: A cube's surface area or volume is given. Its diagonal is asked.
pyqPatterns.approach:
Find the edge first.
Body diagonal = edge × √3.

example.q: The total surface area of a cube is 294 sq cm. Find its body diagonal.
example.solution:
A cube has 6 faces, so one face = 294 ÷ 6 = 49
Edge = √49 = 7
Diagonal = 7 × √3 = **7√3 cm**

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: "How many litres does the tank hold?" or digging cost.
pyqPatterns.approach:
Multiply length × breadth × height in metres.
1 cubic metre = 1000 litres.

example.q: A tank is 1.5 m × 1 m × 0.8 m. How many litres does it hold?
example.solution:
Volume = 1.5 × 1 × 0.8 = 1.2 cubic m
1 cubic m = 1000 litres
1.2 × 1000 = **1200 litres**

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Radius and height of a cylinder. Volume or surface area is asked.
pyqPatterns.approach:
Volume = π × r × r × height.
Curved surface = 2 × π × r × height.

example.q: Find the volume of a cylinder with radius 7 cm and height 10 cm.
example.solution:
Base area = 22/7 × 7 × 7 = 154
Volume = base area × height
= 154 × 10 = **1540 cubic cm**

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: "Radius is doubled and height is halved. What happens to the volume?"
pyqPatterns.approach:
Try a simple radius and height.
Compare old and new volume.

example.q: The radius of a cylinder is doubled and its height halved. Its volume becomes how many times?

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: A pipe with an outer and an inner radius. Volume of metal is asked.
pyqPatterns.approach:
Metal = outer circle area − inner circle area.
Then multiply by the length.

example.q: An iron pipe 14 cm long has outer radius 5 cm and inner radius 3 cm. Find the volume of iron.
example.solution:
Ring area = 22/7 × (5 × 5 − 3 × 3) = 22/7 × 16
Volume = ring area × 14
= 22 × 16 × 2 = **704 cubic cm**

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Radius and height of a cone. Surface area is asked.
pyqPatterns.approach:
Slant height = √(r² + h²). Watch for 7, 24, 25.
Curved surface = π × r × slant height.

example.q: A cone has r = 7 cm and h = 24 cm. Find its curved and total surface area.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: "A solid is melted and made into another shape."
pyqPatterns.approach:
Volume stays the same.
Write both volumes and set them equal.

example.q: A cone of radius 6 cm and height 24 cm is melted into a sphere. Find the sphere's radius.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: A ball, bowl or dome. Surface area or volume is asked.
pyqPatterns.approach:
Sphere surface = 4 × π × r × r.
Sphere volume = 4/3 × π × r × r × r.

example.q: Find the volume of a sphere of radius 21 cm (π = 22/7).

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: A prism, a pyramid or a bucket-shaped solid (frustum). Volume is asked.
pyqPatterns.approach:
Prism: base area × height. Pyramid: one-third of that.
Bucket: ⅓ × π × height × (R×R + r×r + R×r).

example.q: A bucket has radii 5 cm and 3 cm and height 6 cm. Find its capacity.

solvedExamples.q: A room is 12 m long, 9 m wide and 8 m high. Find the length of the longest pole that can be placed inside the room.
solvedExamples.solution:
The longest pole fits along the space diagonal:

$\sqrt{12^2+9^2+8^2}=\sqrt{144+81+64}=\sqrt{289}=17$ m.
solvedExamples.shortcut: 12-9-8 → 17 is a stock diagonal: $144+81+64=289=17^2$. Trap: 15 m is the floor diagonal $\sqrt{12^2+9^2}$.

solvedExamples.q: A cylindrical tank of radius 2 m and depth 7 m is full of water. The capacity of the tank is: [Use $\pi=\frac{22}{7}$]
solvedExamples.solution:
$V=\pi r^2h=\frac{22}{7}\times4\times7=88$ m$^3$.

$1$ m$^3=1000$ litres, so capacity $=88{,}000$ litres.
solvedExamples.shortcut: $88$ m³ ×1000 → 88,000 L. Trap: 880 (×10) or answering in m³.

solvedExamples.q: A solid metallic cone of radius 6 cm and height 3 cm is melted and recast into a sphere. The radius of the sphere is:
solvedExamples.shortcut: $V_{\text{cone}}=36\pi$; set $\frac43\pi R^3=36\pi$ → $R^3=27$ → 3 cm. Trap: 6 cm (radius unchanged) and 2 cm (took $R^3=36/4$ with a slip).

solvedExamples.q: If each edge of a cube increases by 10%, the percentage increase in its volume is:
solvedExamples.solution:
Volume scales as the cube of the linear factor: $(1.1)^3=1.331$.

Increase $=33.1\%$. (Surface would rise by $(1.1)^2=1.21$, i.e. 21%.)

practice.q: The volume of a cube of edge 6 cm is:
practice.shortcut: $6^3=216$. Trap: 36 is the face area.

practice.q: The total surface area of a cuboid of dimensions $8\text{ cm}\times6\text{ cm}\times4\text{ cm}$ is:
practice.shortcut: Half of 208 is 104 — the bracket sum; double it. Trap: 104 (no doubling).

practice.q: The volume of a cylinder of radius 7 cm and height 10 cm is: [Use $\pi=\frac{22}{7}$]
practice.shortcut: $49\times10\times22/7=1540$. Trap: 440 is the CSA ($2\pi rh$).

practice.q: The surface area of a sphere of radius 7 cm is: [Use $\pi=\frac{22}{7}$]
practice.shortcut: $4\times154=616$. Trap: 462 is the hemisphere TSA ($3\pi r^2$); 308 is $2\pi r^2$.

practice.q: The total surface area of a solid hemisphere of radius 7 cm is: [Use $\pi=\frac{22}{7}$]
practice.shortcut: Three circles of $\pi r^2=154$ each → 462. Trap: 308 is only the curved half.

practice.q: The diagonal of a cuboid of dimensions $3\text{ cm}\times4\text{ cm}\times12\text{ cm}$ is:
practice.shortcut: $9+16+144=169=13^2$. This cuboid is a stock triplet (3, 4, 12 → 13).

practice.q: The radius of a cone is 7 cm and its height is 24 cm. Its curved surface area is: [Use $\pi=\frac{22}{7}$]
practice.shortcut: 7-24-25 triplet: $\ell=25$, then $\pi\times7\times25=550$. Trap: 528 uses $h$ instead of $\ell$ ($2\pi rh$).

practice.q: A solid metallic sphere of radius 6 cm is melted and drawn into a cylindrical wire of radius 2 mm. The length of the wire is:
practice.solution:
Sphere: $V=\frac43\pi(6)^3=288\pi$ cu cm.

Wire radius: 2 mm $=0.2$ cm. $V_{\text{wire}}=\pi(0.2)^2L=0.04\pi L$.

$0.04\pi L=288\pi\Rightarrow L=7200$ cm $=72$ m.
practice.shortcut: $288\pi/0.04\pi=7200$ cm. Units trap: 2 mm $=0.2$ cm; answer in metres divides by 100. 720 m forgot that step.

practice.q: A metallic pipe has inner radius 3 cm, outer radius 5 cm and length 14 cm. The volume of metal used is: [Use $\pi=\frac{22}{7}$]
practice.shortcut: Ring area $22\times16=352$, ×14/2... directly: $\frac{22}{7}\times224=704$. Trap: 1100 uses only the outer cylinder.

practice.q: A solid sphere of radius 8 cm is melted and recast into small spheres of radius 1 cm each. The number of small spheres formed is:
practice.shortcut: Cube the radius ratio: $8^3=512$. Trap: 64 (squared the ratio — that is an area ratio).

practice.q: If each edge of a cube increases by 10%, its volume increases by:
practice.shortcut: $1.1^3=1.331$. Trap: 21% is the surface increase; 30% treats volume as linear.

practice.q: A pyramid stands on a square base of side 10 cm and is 12 cm high. Its volume is:
practice.shortcut: $100\times12=1200$, then one-third → 400. Trap: 1200 forgot the $\frac13$.

practice.q: A hemispherical bowl of internal radius 9 cm is full of water. The water is emptied into a cylindrical bottle of radius 3 cm. The height of water in the bottle is: [Use $\pi=\frac{22}{7}$]
practice.shortcut: $486\pi/9\pi=54$. Keep π symbolic — it cancels. Trap: 18 cm uses the bowl volume as $\frac13\pi r^3$.

practice.q: A cube of side 7 cm is painted on all its faces and then cut into 1 cm cubes. How many of the small cubes have exactly two faces painted?
practice.solution: $n=7$: cubes on edges (excluding corners) have exactly two painted faces: $12(n-2)=12\times5=60$.
practice.shortcut: 12 edges × 5 cubes each = 60. Trap: 54 ($6(n-2)^2$ mixing formulas), 75 (5³).

practice.q: A road roller of diameter 84 cm and length 120 cm rolls 500 times over a road. The area of the road levelled is: [Use $\pi=\frac{22}{7}$]
practice.solution:
The roller levels with its curved surface: $CSA=2\pi rh=2\times\frac{22}{7}\times0.42\times1.2=3.168$ sq m.

Area $=500\times3.168=1584$ sq m.
practice.shortcut: CSA in metres ($r=0.42$ m, $h=1.2$ m) is 3.168, then ×500 = 1584. Trap: 3168 doubles it; 792 halves it.

practice.q: The volume of a cuboid of dimensions $8$ cm $\times$ $6$ cm $\times$ $4$ cm is:
practice.shortcut: $lbh = 192$. Trap: adding the dimensions ($18$) or $2(lb+bh+lh)$ when volume is asked.

practice.q: The total surface area of a cuboid of dimensions $12 \times 10 \times 8$ cm is:
practice.shortcut: $2 \times 296 = 592$. Trap: $400$ — that is only $2(lb + bh)$, one face missed.

practice.q: A room is $10$ m long, $6$ m wide and $4$ m high. The area of its four walls is:
practice.shortcut: $2 \times 4 \times (10+6) = 128$. Trap: $240$ (that adds floor + ceiling: $128 + 120$) or $96$ (only $lb \times 2$).

practice.q: The lateral surface area of a cube of side $7$ cm is:
practice.shortcut: Four faces: $196$. Trap: $294$ (six faces) or $343$ (the volume).

practice.q: The sum of the lengths of all edges of a cuboid is $100$ cm and its length, breadth and height are in the ratio $3:2:5$. The length of the cuboid is:
practice.solution:
Edges: $4(l+b+h) = 100 \Rightarrow l+b+h = 25$ cm.

Ratio $3:2:5$ → 10 parts = 25 → 1 part $= 2.5$ cm; length $= 3 \times 2.5 = 7.5$ cm.
practice.shortcut: $l+b+h = 25$; 3 parts of 2.5 = $7.5$ cm. Trap: $10$ cm (the height's 5 parts).

practice.q: The length of the body diagonal of a cube of side $5$ cm is:
practice.shortcut: $5\sqrt3$ (body) vs $5\sqrt2$ (face) — the question says body/longest diagonal.

practice.q: A rectangular tank is $1.5$ m long, $1$ m wide and $0.8$ m deep. Its capacity is:
A pit $10$ m long, $8$ m wide and $2$ m deep is dug. If the cost of digging is Rs $50$ per cu m, the total cost is:
practice.shortcut: Volume first ($160$), then x 50: Rs $8{,}000$. Trap: Rs $1{,}600$ (area x rate).

practice.q: The volume of a cube is $216$ cu cm. Its total surface area is:
practice.shortcut: $a=6$: $6 \times 36 = 216$. (Volume and TSA coincide at $a=6$ — coincidence, not a rule.)

practice.q: The total surface area of a cube is $294$ sq cm. The length of its body diagonal is:
practice.shortcut: TSA → side → diagonal chain: $7\sqrt3$. Trap: $7\sqrt2$ (face diagonal).

practice.q: The volume of a cylinder of radius $7$ cm and height $10$ cm is (take $\pi = 22/7$):
practice.shortcut: $22 \times 7 \times 10 = 1540$. Trap: $770$ (dropped the $r^2$ to $r$).

practice.q: The curved surface area of a cylinder of radius $7$ cm and height $5$ cm is (take $\pi = 22/7$):
practice.shortcut: $44 \times 5 = 220$. Trap: $154$ — that is a $\pi r^2$ piece (one lid).

practice.q: A closed cylindrical drum has radius $7$ cm and height $7$ cm. Its total surface area is (take $\pi = 22/7$):
practice.shortcut: $2\pi r(h+r) = 44 \times 14 = 616$. Trap: $308$ (one lid only).

practice.q: The volume of a cylinder is $1540$ cu cm and the radius of its base is $7$ cm. Its height is (take $\pi = 22/7$):
practice.shortcut: $1540 / 154 = 10$ cm. Trap: $5$ cm (used $2\pi r$ instead of $\pi r^2$).

practice.q: The curved surface area of a cylinder is $352$ sq cm and its height is $8$ cm. Its radius is (take $\pi = 22/7$):
practice.shortcut: $r = \frac{352}{2\pi \times 8} = 7$ cm. Trap: $14$ (forgot the 2 in $2\pi rh$).

practice.q: An iron pipe is $14$ cm long and has an outer radius of $5$ cm and an inner radius of $3$ cm. The volume of iron in the pipe is (take $\pi = 22/7$):
practice.shortcut: Ring $\times$ length: $22/7 \times 16 \times 14 = 704$. Trap: $1100$ (ignored the hollow core).

practice.q: A cylindrical well has a radius of $1.4$ m and a depth of $5$ m. The water it can hold, in litres, is (take $\pi = 22/7$):
practice.shortcut: $30.8\ \text{m}^3 \times 1000 = 30{,}800$ L. Trap: $3{,}080$ (slipped a factor of 10 in $1.4^2$).

practice.q: The radius of a cylinder is doubled and its height is halved. Its volume becomes:
practice.shortcut: $k^2 m = 4 \times \frac12 = 2$: doubled. Trap: 'unchanged' (the $r^2$ and $h$ effects don't cancel).

practice.q: The radius of a cylinder is increased by $50\%$ and its height is decreased by $20\%$. Its volume changes by about:
practice.shortcut: $1.5^2 \times 0.8 = 1.8$ → $+80\%$. Trap: $+50\%$ (applied $1.5 \times 0.8 = 1.2$, missing a radius power).

practice.q: The radius of a cone is $7$ cm and its height is $24$ cm. Its curved surface area is (take $\pi = 22/7$):
practice.shortcut: $l = 25$ first; $\pi r l = 550$. Trap: using $h=24$ in CSA → $528$.

practice.q: The radius of a cone is $7$ cm and its height is $24$ cm. Its volume is (take $\pi = 22/7$):
practice.shortcut: $\frac{1}{3} \times 22 \times 7 \times 24 = 1232$. Trap: $3696$ (forgot the third).

practice.q: The radius of a cone is $7$ cm and its height is $24$ cm. Its total surface area is (take $\pi = 22/7$):
practice.shortcut: $\pi r(l + r) = 22 \times 32 = 704$. Trap: $550$ (CSA only — the tent answer, not this one).

practice.q: The radius of a cone is $7$ cm and its slant height is $10$ cm. Its curved surface area is (take $\pi = 22/7$):
practice.shortcut: $\pi r l$: $220$. Trap: squaring the slant or using $r^2$.

practice.q: The volume of a cone is $132$ cu cm and its base radius is $3$ cm. Its height is (take $\pi = 22/7$):
practice.shortcut: Bring the 3 up: $\frac{3 \times 132}{\frac{22}{7} \times 9} = 14$ cm. Trap: $21$ (used $\frac{V}{\pi r^2}$ without the 3).

practice.q: A solid metallic cone of radius $6$ cm and height $24$ cm is melted and recast into a sphere. The radius of the sphere is (take $\pi = 22/7$):
practice.shortcut: $R^3 = \frac{r^2 h}{4} = 216$ → $R = 6$ cm. Trap: $8$ (set $R^3 = r^2 h$ without the 4).

practice.q: A cylinder and a cone have equal base radii and equal heights. If the volume of the cylinder is $120$ cu cm, the volume of the cone is:
practice.solution: Same base and height: cone $= \frac13 \times$ cylinder $= \frac{120}{3} = 40$ cu cm.
practice.shortcut: One-third: $40$. Trap: $60$ (half) — the hemisphere gets that slot.

practice.q: A cone, a hemisphere and a cylinder stand on equal bases and have the same height. If the volume of the cylinder is $300$ cu cm, the volume of the hemisphere is:
practice.solution:
Same base (radius $r$) and height $h = r$: volumes are $\frac13\pi r^3$, $\frac23\pi r^3$, $\pi r^3$ — ratio $1:2:3$ (cone : hemisphere : cylinder).

Cylinder (3 parts) $= 300$ → 1 part $= 100$; hemisphere $= 2 \times 100 = 200$ cu cm.
practice.shortcut: $\frac{2}{3} \times 300 = 200$. Trap: $100$ (that is the cone's share) or $150$ (splitting $300$ in half).

practice.q: The radius of the base of a cone is $5$ cm and its height is $21$ cm. Its volume is (take $\pi = 22/7$):
practice.shortcut: The 21 and the 7 cancel: $\frac13 \times 21 = 7$. Trap: $770$ (dropped the third).

practice.q: A large metallic cone of height $18$ cm is melted and recast into $27$ small solid cones, each similar in shape to the original. The height of each small cone is:
practice.solution:
Equal shapes: volume ratio $27 = 3^3$ → linear ratio $\sqrt[3]{27} = 3$.

Height $= \frac{18}{3} = 6$ cm.
practice.shortcut: $\sqrt[3]{27} = 3$, so every length divides by 3: $6$ cm. Trap: $2$ cm (dividing by 9, a square root).

practice.q: A heap of wheat is in the shape of a cone. Its base circumference is $44$ m and its height is $3$ m. The volume of the heap is (take $\pi = 22/7$):
practice.shortcut: Circumference → $r = 7$; then a third: $154$. Trap: $462$ (full cylinder volume).

practice.q: A conical tent has a base radius of $7$ m and a slant height of $25$ m. If canvas costs Rs $2$ per sq m, the cost of the canvas needed to make the tent is (take $\pi = 22/7$):
practice.solution:
Canvas covers the curved surface only: CSA $= \pi r l = \frac{22}{7} \times 7 \times 25 = 550$ sq m.

Cost $= 550 \times 2 = 1100$.
practice.shortcut: CSA $550 \times$ Rs $2$ = Rs $1{,}100$. Trap: Rs $1{,}232$ — that is the volume number, a different measure.

practice.q: The surface area of a sphere of radius $7$ cm is (take $\pi = 22/7$):
practice.shortcut: $4 \times 22 \times 7 = 616$. Trap: $308$ (half — the hemisphere CSA) or $462$ (hemisphere TSA).

practice.q: The volume of a sphere of radius $21$ cm is (take $\pi = 22/7$):
The curved surface area of a hemisphere of radius $7$ cm is (take $\pi = 22/7$):
practice.shortcut: Half the sphere: $308$. Trap: $462$ — that adds the flat circular face.

practice.q: The total surface area of a solid hemisphere of radius $7$ cm is (take $\pi = 22/7$):
practice.shortcut: Curved $308$ + flat face $154$ = $462$. Trap: $308$ (forgetting the lid) or $770$ (wrong $4\pi r^2 + \pi r^2$).

practice.q: A solid metal sphere of radius $6$ cm is melted and drawn into $8$ equal small spheres. The radius of each small sphere is:
practice.solution:
$8 = 2^3$ equal spheres → each length divides by $\sqrt[3]{8} = 2$.

Radius $= \frac{6}{2} = 3$ cm.
practice.shortcut: $r = 6/\sqrt[3]{8} = 3$ cm. Trap: $2$ cm (dividing the radius by 3, the wrong root).

practice.q: A solid sphere of radius $3$ cm is dropped into a cylindrical vessel of base radius $4$ cm containing water. The height by which the water rises is (take $\pi = 22/7$):
practice.shortcut: $h = \frac{V}{\pi R^2} = \frac{36}{16} = 2.25$ cm. Trap: $3$ cm (confusing the sphere's radius with the rise).

practice.q: If the radius of a sphere is doubled, its surface area becomes:
practice.shortcut: $k^2 = 4$. Trap: $8$ times — that is the VOLUME's multiplier ($k^3$).

practice.q: The radii of two spheres are in the ratio $3:4$. The ratio of their volumes is:
practice.solution: Volumes scale as the cube of the radius ratio: $3^3 : 4^3 = 27 : 64$.
practice.shortcut: $27:64$ (cube the ratio). Trap: $9:16$ — that is the surface-area ratio.

practice.q: A triangular prism has a cross-sectional area of $20$ sq cm and a length of $12$ cm. Its volume is:
practice.shortcut: Area x length. Trap: $120$ (a stray half — prisms carry no $\frac13$ or $\frac12$ factor).

practice.q: A rectangular tank measures $5$ m $\times$ $4$ m $\times$ $3$ m. Its capacity in litres is:
practice.shortcut: $60\ \text{m}^3 \times 1000$ = $60{,}000$ L. Trap: $6{,}000$ (a slipped zero).

practice.q: A pyramid stands on a square base of side $10$ cm and has a height of $12$ cm. Its volume is:
practice.shortcut: One-third of $1200 = 400$. Trap: $1200$ — the containing prism's volume.

practice.q: A pyramid has a rectangular base $12$ cm $\times$ $9$ cm and a height of $10$ cm. Its volume is:
practice.shortcut: $\frac13 \times 1080 = 360$. Trap: $1080$ (no third) — one step, one mark.

practice.q: A bucket is shaped like a frustum of a cone with end radii $5$ cm and $3$ cm and depth $6$ cm. Its capacity is (take $\pi = 22/7$):
practice.shortcut: $\frac{6}{3} = 2$; $2 \times \frac{22}{7} \times 49 = 308$. Trap: $264$ — the missing $Rr = 15$ term.

practice.q: A tumbler is a frustum of a cone with radii $4$ cm and $2$ cm and height $21$ cm. Its volume is (take $\pi = 22/7$):
practice.shortcut: $\frac{21}{3} = 7$; $22 \times 28 = 616$. Trap: $440$ (dropping the $Rr = 8$ term).

practice.q: A wooden cube of side $4$ cm is cut into unit cubes (edge $1$ cm). How many small cubes are formed?
practice.shortcut: $4^3 = 64$. Trap: $16$ — that is one FACE of small cubes ($4^2$).

practice.q: Three metallic cubes of edges $3$ cm, $4$ cm and $5$ cm are melted and recast into a single cube. The edge of the new cube is:
practice.shortcut: $\sqrt[3]{216} = 6$ cm. Trap: $12$ cm (the SUM of edges instead of the cube root of the volume sum).

practice.q: A triangular prism has a perimeter of $12$ cm for its cross-section and a length of $10$ cm. Its lateral surface area is:
practice.shortcut: The tube unrolls to $12 \times 10$. Trap: $60$ (a spurious half).

practice.q: A square pyramid has a base edge of $10$ cm and a slant height of $13$ cm. Its lateral surface area is:
practice.solution: Perimeter $= 40$; LSA $= \frac12 P l = \frac12 \times 40 \times 13 = 260$ sq cm.
practice.shortcut: $\frac12 \times 40 \times 13 = 260$. Trap: $520$ (forgot the half) — four triangles, halved each.
